messages.body_plain:
Hello Dr. Broman and the R/qtl community -

I was hoping that I could get some insight on the generation of a negative LOD score generated from the scanone function with a binary trait model generated using HK.

Specifically, I have one marker with a negative LOD score that is sandwiched between two markers with LOD scores > 30. There might be a recombination event or two between the consecutive markers (markers are 500 kb genomic bins genotyped with low coverage sequencing), but the genotypes aren't that different from one marker to the next. Given how I did the genotyping, if a recombination event happened in a bin, I scored that bin as missing data rather than assigning it a genotype, so maybe that particular marker has more missing data points, but I don't think that it varies much (I realize that I could get counts on the missing data, but I don't think it's likely to be substantially different). Would that likely cause the negative LOD score?

I have room to improve in my statistical knowledge and I tried looking into what the code for the scanone function (using getAnywhere) is to see if I could understand it better and figure out what it's actually doing, but I got lost in all of the if/thens. I don't think that the problem occurs if the data aren't analyzed with a binary model.

In a manual somewhere I saw that LOD is calculated as n/2 * log10(RSS0/RSS1). In my head, I read this as if the null hypothesis of no QTL (RSS0) is more likely than the alternative of a single QTL (RSS1), then the ratio would be greater than 1 and taking the log should generate a positive value and that a negative LOD would be generated when a single QTL is more likely than no QTL. What am I missing as it seems like it should be the other way around?

Also, the trait that I'm mapping appears to be a single locus Mendelian trait (based on phenotype frequencies), but when I map it, I get a second peak that appears to be fairly substantial. Looking more closely at the data, I realize that this is likely caused by some sort of DMI - for example, there are no individuals homozygous for one parent at one locus and homozygous for the other parent at the other locus. In order to show that the second locus is most likely due to a genetic incompatibility, I used the genotype at the main locus as a covariate. This eliminated the association between genotype and phenotype at the second locus and also resulted in lots of negative LOD scores at other parts of the genome. Spoiler alert, I already ID'ed the gene that's causing the phenotype (yeah), but am trying to make a nice figure of what happens when I control for the genotype at the main locus. For good measure, I did see what happened when I used the genotype at the second locus as a covariate for the main locus and we're all good.

Any help with understanding what is happening would be greatly appreciated! I'm attaching an image as an example.

Thanks, Anji

My guess is that this is a convergence problem, perhaps due to perfect genotype/phenotype association at this position. Binary trait analysis requires an iterative algorithm, where you start with initial estimates of the QTL effects and then get improved estimates in each of successive iterations, until the algorithm converges.

Perhaps try messing around with the maxit and tol parameters. You might need to do a custom analysis to get correct results for that one position.

Congrats on finding the gene!

messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I am quite new to QTL mapping and currently try to construct a genetic map for a plant species from F2 cross.

The background is the following:
The data is represented by 140 F2 progeny individuals + 2 homozygous parents genotyped at all positions, 6310 SNPs after all filtering procedures in TASSEL.
I run all filtering procedures from "genetic map construction" tutorial including filtering for duplicate SNPs and segregation pattern (p < 0.05/#of obs.). As a result I have around 137 individuals and 3K SNPs left, ~150 markers per chromosome on average.
Since I have a prior knowledge on the the linkage groups I did not try to form them from scratch, furthermore by reading the forum I understood that if the genome is assembled one should not try to reconstruct the LGs.
Thus I started to order the markers and for each chromosome I had the following picture:

As you can see there are several gaps with low LOD scores at the ends of the chromosome before ordering and similar gaps in the middle of chromosome after ordering. Furthermore the genetic map is implausibly large ~1200 cM. By the way est.map() produced even worth result thus I refused to use it and used orderMarkers() with Kosambi mapping function (Haldane produced a bit larger map of 1400 cM).

What I already tried to do in order to to remove such gaps:
-remove pairs of distant markers located at more than 30 cM after running allchrsplits()
-remove markers that that demonstrated high LOD scores (>-20) after running droponemarker()
All of these attempts were followed by re running orderMarkers() with Kosambi mapping function. And both of these methods failed to significantly reduce the length of the chromosome.

What I want to do is intuitively get rid of the gaps with low LOD scores, since I guess that these are the reasons for such huge chromosome lengths but I don't know how to do that correctly with R/qtl functions. I suspect that these gaps are the result of noisy GBS data, but despite strict filtering they somehow remain in dataset.

So I wonder if someone already faced such or similar problem with GBS data analysis? And what were your solutions to remove such "noisy" markers and fix the chromosome length?

Sincerely,
Rim

messages.body_plain:
I would start with your physical map, and use some estimate of the cM/Mbp relation for your organism to get an approximate genetic map.

If you want to re-estimate the inter-marker distances with your genotype data, it's better to start with the physical order. Determining order from scratch should bring you back to the same place, and you'll still need to estimate the inter-marker distances.

The data cleaning to fix problems in the estimated map can be difficult. I guess I'd first look at segregation distortion. Then I'd look at the markers adjacent to any huge intervals: if you drop one of those markers, does the interval shrink? This is what the droponemarker() is supposed to help with.

karl

messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] How to load a BC1HD crosstype with qtl::read.cross()
messages.body_plain:
The cross type defines
(a) the possible genotypes
(b) the frequency of exchange between markers, and
(c) the relative frequency of the genotypes
which are then used to calculate the probability of each possible genotype in each individual at each position in the genome.

In a BC1DH population, you'd have a skewing of genotypes from 1:1 in a regular DH plus a greater density of crossovers, but if the genotypes are dense and complete, the model for the (b) frequency of exchanges and (c) relative frequency of genotypes wouldn't have much influence.

karl

I considered using marker regression but it seems i would be losing a lot of individuals, as it omits any individual with any amount of missing gt data.

summary(out.all, perms = operm.all, format = "tabByCol", alpha = p_value, pvalues = TRUE)

if there a way to force the "summary" command to consider QTLs only among my list of actual markers, while using interval mapping techniques?
if not, what is the best way to accomplish my goal?

thank you in advance!

messages.body_plain:
When looking at the genotype frequencies at markers, we’re trying to distinguish between “real” biologic deviation from Mendel’s rules, where it should be that all of the markers on a chromosome are deviating in the same way. If you see that, all is fine. I’d say a marker looks bad if it’s behaving quite differently from those around it.

But if you don’t know the order of markers, it can be hard to tell between these cases. Requires a bit of trial and error.

karl
